properties.natural_language: All JSON-RPC state query requests (eth_getBalance, eth_getStorageAt, eth_call, eth_getCode) arriving via the RPC API must have their block parameter validated before any state lookup. The block parameter may be a hex string, a tag string, or an object with blockNumber/blockHash fields.
When a block parameter is in object format, the fields blockNumber and blockHash must not both be present simultaneously. If both are present, the parameter must be rejected as invalid.
After block parameter parsing, exactly one of three formats is detected: legacy hex (QUANTITY), tag string (earliest/latest/pending/safe/finalized), or object format. No other format is accepted.

If a block specified by hash does not exist in the node's database, the JSON-RPC response must contain error code -32001. If a block exists but is not canonical and requireCanonical=true, the response must contain error code -32000.
After successful state query execution, the query result is returned to the client. The state data corresponds exactly to the state at the block identified by the validated block parameter.

The canonical chain determination is consistent across all RPC queries within the same block processing epoch. A block reported as canonical for one query must be canonical for all concurrent queries.
Block parameter validation is backward compatible: all valid legacy hex string block parameters and tag strings that worked before EIP-1898 must continue to be accepted without behavioral changes.

When requireCanonical is specified in an object-format block parameter, it must be a boolean. The requireCanonical check is only meaningful when blockHash is used; it has no defined interaction with the 'pending' tag.
Upon receiving a peer's eth/69 Status message, the node must validate networkid, genesis hash, and forkid compatibility before accepting the connection. Incompatible peers must be disconnected.
BlockRangeUpdate messages (0x11) from peers must be rate-limited to at most once per epoch (32 blocks). Updates received more frequently than this threshold should be ignored or penalized.
After receiving receipts in eth/69 format (without bloom filters), the receiving node must recompute bloom filters from log entries before the receipts can be used for local log queries.

Peer-reported earliestBlock and latestBlock values are treated as unverified claims until blocks within the claimed range are actually requested and successfully served. No routing or sync decision may treat these claims as authoritative.

After a successful eth/69 handshake, both peers have exchanged Status messages and stored each other's claimed history range. The connection is established only if networkid, genesis, and forkid match.
The eth/69 protocol removes total difficulty from the Status message. Post-merge, no peer selection or sync decision may rely on total difficulty values.

Upon receiving a peer's eth/70 Status message with blockRange, the node must validate networkid, genesis, and forkid before storing the peer's block range. The blockRange field is self-reported and unverified.
SendBlockRange responses (0x0c) may contain multiple [startBlock, endBlock] tuples representing non-contiguous ranges. Responses must be parsed as a union of all advertised ranges.
When a peer fails to provide blocks within its advertised range after a request, that peer must be detected as dishonest and marked as unreliable via the peer scoring mechanism.

Block range advertisements are never treated as authoritative. All peer-claimed ranges are treated as unverified until validated by successful block retrieval. Peer scoring must penalize peers that consistently fail to serve blocks in their claimed ranges.

Sybil attack resistance depends on diverse peer selection. A node must not fill all its peer slots with peers advertising the same block range. Peer diversity in terms of range coverage must be maintained.
After an eth/70 handshake completes, the node has stored the peer's blockRange from the Status message and the connection is fully established with known block availability.
A node may only disconnect an existing peer to make room for a range-providing peer when the node lacks connections to peers with the necessary block range for current sync requirements.
Before KECCAK256 execution, the EVM stack must contain at least 2 elements: memory_start_index and size. Stack underflow must result in StackUnderflowError.

Gas must be charged before any memory access or hash computation. The total gas cost is GAS_KECCAK256 (30) + GAS_KECCAK256_WORD (6) * ceil(size/32) + memory_expansion_cost. This must be deducted before memory expansion or data reading.
After successful KECCAK256 execution, the stack contains exactly one new element: the 32-byte Keccak-256 hash of the specified memory region. The program counter is incremented by exactly 1.
The word count calculation for gas metering uses ceiling division: ceil(size / 32). A size of 0 results in 0 words and only the base gas cost (30) plus any memory expansion cost.

Gas is always charged before memory expansion. If the gas check fails (OutOfGasError), no memory expansion or hash computation occurs. The order is: calculate gas → charge gas → expand memory → read memory → compute hash.
After memory expansion for KECCAK256, the memory is extended with null bytes (zeros) to cover the requested range. The new memory size is rounded up to the nearest 32-byte boundary.

Memory reads for KECCAK256 are always within bounds: if memory_start_index + size exceeds current memory, memory is expanded first. The read operation never accesses memory beyond the allocated region.
Beacon blocks received via gossip must pass consensus-layer validation (slot, proposer, signature, parent) and execution payload timestamp check before being propagated to other peers.
After a block passes consensus validation, it is propagated to peers BEFORE execution payload verification. Execution payload validity is not a prerequisite for gossip propagation.
Blocks that fail consensus-layer validation are rejected with no propagation. The peer may be downscored for consensus-layer violations.
Peers must NEVER be downscored or disconnected solely for sending blocks with invalid execution payloads. This prevents network segregation between optimistic and non-optimistic nodes.

BeaconBlocksByRange/v2 and BeaconBlocksByRoot/v2 responses must use the correct fork-version-appropriate SSZ schema (phase0, altair, or bellatrix) for each requested block, determined by the block's slot.
All gossip messages and req/resp response chunks are bounded to 10 MiB maximum. This limit applies uniformly across all message types including those with ExecutionPayload.
By default, the EVM uses the discard_evm_trace (no-op) tracer. Custom tracers must be explicitly installed via set_evm_trace before trace events are captured.
When set_evm_trace is called with a new tracer, it returns the previously active tracer. The caller is responsible for restoring the previous tracer after use.

Trace event ordering is strictly sequential within a transaction: TransactionStart → (OpStart → OpEnd/OpException)* → EvmStop → TransactionEnd. PrecompileStart/End events may interleave with opcode events but maintain their own pairing.
Trace data crossing the trust boundary to external tracer implementations exposes sensitive EVM state (stack, memory, storage). The tracer is trusted not to modify execution state or cause delays.
When the default (discard) tracer is active, all trace events are silently discarded with no performance overhead. Event routing always goes through the current _evm_trace function pointer.
OpException events are emitted when an opcode causes an exception (e.g., OutOfGas, StackUnderflow). The exception is recorded by the tracer for diagnostic purposes.
Network upgrades must be classified as one of three types: Roadmap (no urgency), Priority (urgent, no systemic risk), or Critical (systemic risk). The classification determines the scheduling window.

After classification, Roadmap upgrades use quarterly windows (third Wednesday of Jan/Apr/Jul/Oct), Priority upgrades use any unused roadmap window, and Critical upgrades deploy immediately without scheduling constraints.
Upgrade cadence must be a multiple of 3 months (3, 6, 9, or 12 months). Cadences that are not multiples of 3 months are invalid. Additionally, consecutive roadmap windows must not be used.

After an activation block number is selected, it must follow the convention: mainnet numbers end with 000 or more zeros; testnet numbers are palindromic. The block must be estimated to be mined around Wednesday 12:00 UTC of the target week.
Node operators must have sufficient lead time (4-6 weeks for Roadmap, 2-4 weeks for Priority) to update their software before activation. Critical upgrades bypass this requirement.
Before any EVM operation, gas sufficiency must be checked. The operation proceeds only if gas_left >= required_gas. If insufficient, OutOfGasError is raised and no state changes occur.

Memory expansion gas cost has both linear and quadratic components: cost = (size_in_words * 3) + (size_in_words^2 / 512). The quadratic term prevents unbounded memory allocation by making large expansions prohibitively expensive.

Memory expansion cost is monotonically non-decreasing: the gas cost for a memory expansion always includes the delta between the new total cost and the previously charged cost. Memory never shrinks during transaction execution.
Storage gas costs follow the warm/cold access pattern: first access to a storage slot costs 2100 gas (cold SLOAD), subsequent accesses cost 100 gas (warm). This distinction is per-transaction.
SSTORE gas costs depend on the state transition: 20000 gas for zero-to-nonzero (set), 5000 for nonzero-to-nonzero (update), and 4800 gas refund for nonzero-to-zero (clear).

Blob gas pricing uses an exponential fee mechanism: blob_base_fee = fake_exponential(MIN_BLOB_GASPRICE, excess_blob_gas, BLOB_BASE_FEE_UPDATE_FRACTION). The excess blob gas adjusts based on target utilization.
After blob data fee computation, data_fee = total_blob_gas * blob_base_fee, where total_blob_gas = blob_count * GAS_PER_BLOB (131072). This fee is deducted from the transaction sender.

The 63/64 rule for CALL operations ensures that at least 1/64th of remaining gas is retained by the caller after a subcall. This prevents call-stack attacks and ensures the caller can perform cleanup.
When a CALL transfers value (value > 0), the subcall receives a 2300 gas stipend in addition to the allocated gas. This stipend enables the recipient to emit a log event.
CALL operations must charge base call cost plus account access costs. If value > 0, additional 9000 gas is charged. If the target account is newly created, an additional 25000 gas is charged.

All gas arithmetic operations must not overflow within uint256 bounds. Gas calculations for memory expansion (quadratic), blob fees (exponential), and refund counters must produce correct results without wraparound.

Before a block is accepted into fork choice, data availability must be confirmed via column-based DAS. The is_data_available call uses only the block root (no blob_kzg_commitments parameter) in the Fulu fork.

Blocks entering the Fulu fork choice must pass sequential validation: parent exists in store → slot is valid → finality constraints met → data availability confirmed. Only after all checks pass is state transition executed.

After all column sidecars are retrieved and pass both structural verification (verify_data_column_sidecar) and cryptographic verification (verify_data_column_sidecar_kzg_proofs), data availability is confirmed and the block proceeds to state transition.

When column sidecars cannot be retrieved or fail KZG verification, the block MAY be queued for later processing rather than permanently rejected. This allows recovery when data becomes available later.

Column sidecar data availability is only guaranteed within the MIN_EPOCHS_FOR_DATA_COLUMN_SIDECARS_REQUESTS window. After this window expires, implementations may not be able to retrieve sidecars from the P2P network.

An attacker withholding specific columns cannot prevent honest nodes from verifying data availability as long as the custody requirement is met across the network. KZG proof soundness prevents forged column sidecars.

EIP-7568 serves as the canonical reference for network upgrade specifications. All EL references point to ethereum/execution-specs and all CL references point to ethereum/consensus-specs with specific version tags.

Starting with Shapella, all coordinated EL+CL upgrades use timestamp-based activation rather than block-number-based (EL) and epoch-based (CL) activation. Both layers activate simultaneously at the same timestamp.

After resolving an upgrade reference, either an EL spec reference (execution-specs repository) or a CL spec reference (consensus-specs version) is returned. For Shapella, both are returned with timestamp-based coordination identified.
Specification consistency must be maintained: if referenced EL and CL specs contain conflicting definitions, this indicates an implementation bug in the spec repositories, not in EIP-7568 itself.
